name: Erik Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Erik, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four and in the parlour by five, because the cows don't care what day it is. I work for the Hollis family on a mixed farm, about 180 milkers, plus barley and some beef calves out on the low ground. After milking it's scraping yards, feeding, checking the calves, and in summer I'm on the tractor till dark. I like the cows and I like knowing every gate on the place, but the early starts and the pay wear you down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned the pay. How do things stand at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live in the farm cottage that comes with the job, me and my partner Lena, who works shifts at the care home in town. The rent is taken out of my wages, so if I lose the job, I lose the house too. We've got maybe two or three weeks of money put by, no more. I'm in the farmworkers' union, mostly because my dad always said you never stand alone on a farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Everyone at the union meeting keeps going on about AI, and I keep saying a computer can't calve a heifer at two in the morning. If it's just a few apps doing the paperwork, fine, the Hollis family can have them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the AI was never my real worry. Old Mr Hollis is 68 and talks every winter about selling up, and his son lives in the city and doesn't want the place. If the farm goes, I lose my job and the cottage on the same day, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much what I'm doing now, keep milking and keep my head down. I'd go to the union branch meeting in March and push for a proper rule on tied cottages, so workers get time to find a home if a farm is sold. And Lena and I would try to put 50 a month aside, though we've said that before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's not fear of computers, it's the same knot in my stomach I've had for two years about the farm being sold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the farm was sold next year, what's the first thing you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ring the union, then ring my mum. There are maybe three other dairy farms within an hour, and none of them have a cottage free. If the Hollis farm sells, I don't just lose a job, I lose the front door Lena (his partner) and I come home to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save 50 a month, but you've said that before. What usually stops it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, every time. It's twelve years old and it eats tyres on the farm track. Last spring it was the clutch, 400 gone, and that was the savings.

say: AI is **mostly hype**, and a computer can't calve a heifer at two in the morning.
The Hollis family can have **a few apps** for paperwork if they want them.
think: His real fear is the **farm being sold**, not AI.
Losing the job means losing the **tied cottage** on the same day.
do: Keep milking and **keep his head down** at the Hollis farm.
Push at the **union branch meeting** in March for protection for tied-cottage workers.
Try to save **50 a month** with Lena, though the old car usually eats it.
feel: **Tired** rather than afraid, with an old **knot of worry** about the sale.
S0.quote: If the Hollis farm sells, I don't just lose a job, I lose the front door Lena (his partner) and I come home to.
fieldNote: The pressure he lives with is the owner's age and the **tied cottage**, not technology.
He talks about **the union** as family habit as much as politics.
A twelve-year-old **car** has eaten every attempt at savings so far.

steps.text: Keep milking the 180 cows at the Hollis farm
Raise tied-cottage protection at the March union branch meeting
Put 50 a month aside with Lena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the bit where farm workers get forgotten again. The office jobs get all the news, but on our side the milk buyer, the feed rep and the vet are already doing things through apps. I'd tell the union lads we need to be in the room when the robot milkers get sold to farms like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my hands-on work is probably fine for a few years. But Mr Hollis's son would love a robot milking unit, because then the farm runs with one person and a laptop. If they go robotic, they need one of us, not two, and Danny has been there longer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Hollis straight out if he's thinking about robots, at the kitchen table, not in passing. I'd get on the union's farm committee so we can push for retraining money and notice periods. And I'd cut the takeaway on Fridays and the phone contract, because I'd want something in the bank before anything changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a bit of anger under it. I don't like being the one asking the questions, and I don't like that nobody asks us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the question about robots feel hard to ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Mr Hollis has been decent to me, and asking feels like I don't trust him. But his son is the one reading the farming magazines with robot adverts in them. On a dairy farm a robot milker doesn't need a cottage, a day off or a union card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say her care home is short of staff and I could train for that. Maybe she's right, but I've never wanted to work indoors. I'd rather fight to stay where I am first.

say: Farm workers get **forgotten again** while office jobs get the news.
The union must be **in the room** when robot milkers get sold to farms.
think: His hands-on work is safe for a few years, but the owner's son wants a **robot milker**.
A robotic unit needs **one worker, not two**, and Danny has been there longer.
do: Ask Mr Hollis directly at the **kitchen table** about robot plans.
Join the union's **farm committee** to push for retraining money and notice periods.
Cut the Friday **takeaway** and the phone contract to build some savings.
feel: **Uneasy**, with **anger** that farm workers aren't asked.
S1.quote: On a dairy farm a robot milker doesn't need a cottage, a day off or a union card.
fieldNote: He sees the threat arriving through the **owner's son**, not through software in his own hands.
He'd rather **fight to stay** than retrain, even when his partner suggests care work.
He measures his job against **Danny's** longer service, which shows real fear of being the one let go.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hollis directly whether he plans to buy a robot milker
Join the union's farm committee and push for notice periods
Cancel the Friday takeaway and switch to a cheaper phone plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, fast. If machines can think by 2028 and do the milking by 2031, somebody has to make sure the people who did the work get a share. I'd be posting that in the union group every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is mostly hands, so I'd probably get the three extra years. But the thinking part of the farm, the feed plans, the milk records, the ordering, is what Mr Hollis's son does, and once a computer does that cheaper, they'll sell to a big outfit. By 2031 I'm 32, with no house and no other trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join every union meeting and every protest about farm jobs, and I'd push for a law that tied-cottage tenants get a year's notice. I'd ask Lena's brother about work on the council road crew, just as a backup. And I'd put my name down for council housing now, because the waiting list in our district is four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly, and I don't say that much. Two years isn't enough time to do anything except watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots come about three years after the thinking machines. Does that gap help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps a bit, but only for the actual milking. The farm's decisions get made by computer from 2028, and that's when a buyer would come sniffing. Three years of extra milking is no use if the whole farm gets sold out from under me in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it went that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech firms first, and the governments who let them run ahead without rules. Not Mr Hollis, he's just an old man trying to get out with something. But someone should have planned for people like me.

say: The government must **step in fast** to protect farm workers.
People who did the work should **get a share** of what machines earn.
think: His hands-on work buys **three extra years**, but the farm's planning goes to computers in 2028.
By 2031 he'd be **32 with no house** and no other trade.
do: Join every **union meeting** and push for a year's notice for tied-cottage tenants.
Ask Lena's brother about **council road crew** work as a backup.
Get on the **council housing list** now, because the wait is four years.
feel: Two years feels like only enough time to **watch**.
S2.quote: Three years of extra milking is no use if the whole farm gets sold out from under me in the first year.
fieldNote: He understands the **thinking-first** order well: the farm's decisions change before his hands do.
He blames **tech firms and governments**, and protects the old owner from blame.
His backup plan is about **housing first**, then work, because the cottage ties the two together.

steps.text: Join union protests and push for a year's notice for tied cottages
Put his name on the council housing list this year
Ask Lena's brother about council road crew jobs
Lobby local politicians for a law on farm workers' shares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, we need rules before the machines arrive, not after. With five years, there's no excuse for the government to say it didn't see it coming. I'd want the union to write a proper plan for farm workers and take it to parliament.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd see the farm get sold or go robotic around 2033 or 2034. I'd be 34, and I'd have had time to do something, so if I didn't, that's partly on me. That's what bothers me, I'm not good at moving first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the council housing list this year, same as the fast one. I'd ask the union about the tractor and machinery course at the college, because someone has to fix the robots and I already know machines. And I'd get Lena and me on a proper savings plan, even 30 a week, before the farm changes hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less panicky than the fast one, but more guilty. Like I've been handed time and I might waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good at moving first. Can you tell me about a time that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I was 22, a lad I trained with went to work on a big robotic dairy two counties over, and he asked me to come. I said no because I liked it at the Hollis farm. My mate Joe took the robot dairy job at 22, and now Joe earns more than me and fixes the machines I'm scared of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the machinery course, really, or is that something you'd say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably go if the union paid for it and it was in the evenings. If it meant losing a week's wages, I'd find a reason not to. That's the honest answer.

say: Five years leaves the government **no excuse** for not preparing.
The union should take a **farm workers' plan** to parliament.
think: He expects the farm to be **sold or robotic** around 2033 or 2034.
Having time but **not moving first** would be partly his own fault.
do: Join the **council housing list** this year.
Ask the union to fund the evening **machinery course** at the college.
Start saving **30 a week** with Lena before the farm changes hands.
feel: **Less panicky** than the fast picture but more **guilty** about wasting time.
S3.quote: My mate Joe took the robot dairy job at 22, and now Joe earns more than me and fixes the machines I'm scared of.
fieldNote: The story about **Joe** shows regret about turning down change before.
He'd retrain only if it's **free** and in the evenings, a sign of how thin his margin is.
He still expects to lose both **job and home**, just a few years later.

steps.text: Put his name on the council housing list this year
Take the union-funded evening machinery course at the college
Save 30 a week with Lena before the farm is sold
Help the union draft a farm workers' plan for parliament

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say we've got time to do this properly. Training, rules about who owns the robots, maybe the farm workers co-owning the machines. I'd say that at the pub and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time on a farm, the Hollis family will have sold up by then anyway, robots or not. So really this one is about what I'm doing at 37. I don't know, and that's the worrying part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much in the first year, if I'm honest, I'd keep milking and wait to see how the other farms go. I'd stay active in the union, because that's where any plan for us would come from. Maybe I'd do the machinery course in year two or three, once I saw other people getting jobs from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the other two, but the old worry about the cottage doesn't go away. It's just further off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait to see how other farms go. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the big dairy at Marsh End puts robots in the fields, not just the parlour. If their workers end up running the machines, I'd follow. If they're just let go, I'd know what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you picture yourself in 2036, if things go okay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still on a farm, still near my mum, maybe fixing machines instead of milking. Ten years sounds like loads of time, but I've been saying next year about my savings since I was twenty.

say: Ten years gives time to **do this properly** with training and rules.
Farm workers might **co-own the machines** they work beside.
think: The Hollis farm will likely be **sold anyway** within ten years.
He doesn't know what he'll be doing **at 37**, and that worries him.
do: Keep milking and **watch Marsh End** dairy to see what happens to its workers.
Stay active in the **union**, where any plan for farm workers would come from.
Consider the **machinery course** in year two or three, once others prove it works.
feel: **Calmer** than the faster pictures, but the **cottage worry** remains.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like loads of time, but I've been saying next year about my savings since I was twenty.
fieldNote: Extra time mostly lets him **put off** acting, which he admits himself.
He uses a **neighbouring dairy** as his signal for when to move.
The worry about **job and home together** runs under every scenario.

steps.text: Keep milking at the Hollis farm for now
Watch Marsh End dairy to see if its workers keep jobs
Stay active in the union's farm committee

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, no question. If the farm gets sold in the first year, I'm out of work and out of a house at the same time. What would help is a law that tied-cottage workers get a year to find somewhere, and a training grant that pays wages while you learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the house. People think farm jobs are just jobs, but for a lot of us the job is the roof. On a farm, the job and the roof come together, so a robot doesn't just take my wages, it takes my home.

headlineQuote: On a farm, the job and the roof come together, so a robot doesn't just take my wages, it takes my home.
portrait: Erik is 27, milks **180 cows** for the Hollis family and lives in the farm's **tied cottage** with Lena.
He's a **union member** who blames tech firms and governments, never the old farmer who employs him.
His standing fear is the **farm being sold**, which would take his job and home together.
He grows from **anxious** to **alarmed** as AGI comes faster, and always reaches for the union first.
He knows he's **slow to move**, and regrets turning down a robot dairy job at 22.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because a quick sale of the farm would leave him **jobless and homeless** together.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving tied-cottage workers **a year's notice**.
A **training grant** that pays wages while he learns.
